title: Making Sense of School
author: Matthew Evans
summary: This extract from Matthew Evans's book 'Making Sense of School' asks why the purpose of schools is so contested by working backward through a brief history of formal education. Evans argues that schools exist to educate children 'so that...' -- and that the impossibility of completing that sentence with a single agreed answer explains decades of curriculum and pedagogy wars. Tracing schooling from ancient Rome's communal gatherings through Greek leadership preparation, Spartan military discipline, Indian Vedic and Buddhist curricula, medieval charitable education, and Horace Mann's 19th-century American Common Schools, Evans shows that every era layered a new 'so that' onto the institution without discarding the old ones. Mann's Common Schools added the concepts of efficiency (low unit-cost at scale), equality (every child's right to education), and social engineering (all classes taught together) -- concepts still embedded in modern schooling and still in tension with each other. The piece's animating argument is that the contested purpose of schools is not an accident but the inevitable result of an institution asked to carry too many different social functions at once, each inherited from a different historical moment and none ever fully replaced.
points: The contested purpose of modern schooling is a historical accumulation: every era added 'so that' clauses (citizenship, economic growth, equality, moral formation) without removing the older ones, leaving schools carrying irreconcilable mandates.

Ancient schools already introduced the core tension: education for different children with different purposes (Greek rhetoric for leaders vs. Spartan obedience for soldiers) meant 'education' never had a single definition.

Horace Mann's Common Schools embedded three principles -- efficiency, equality, and social engineering -- that remain structurally present in modern schooling and frequently pull against each other in practice.

Medieval charitable education added moral formation and workforce preparation from wealthy endowments through industrial-era factory schools -- motivations still visible in modern schools' stated aims and values.
The deeper rationale beneath all 'so that' clauses is the societal function of knowledge transmission: passing what each generation knows to the next so the species can thrive.
quotes: The function of a school is also simple: it is to educate children. But try to complete the sentence 'Schools educate children so that...'. I expect you end up with quite a long list, not all of which we might agree upon. This is what people mean when they say that the purpose of school is contested.

Throughout human evolution, the social transmission of knowledge has been required. One generation must pass what it knows onto the next if the species is to survive. Education therefore became not just about surviving, but about thriving, and not just about families, but about society.
Ancient Greece introduces us to the idea that schooling can prepare different groups to play different roles in society.

The invention of modern schooling is often credited to an American, Horace Mann. The mass education of an entire population of children embedded three important concepts: efficiency, because educating children at this scale was expensive and a low unit-cost must be achieved; equality because Mann believed every child had a right to be educated; social engineering because all classes should be taught together.

Is it any wonder the purpose of modern schools is contested? We may argue that the purpose of schools is to educate children so that they inherit the world's knowledge, so that society thrives, so that children can play a role in society, so that the economy grows, so that people live fulfilling lives.

In the middle-ages, the church began to educate poor children as a charitable enterprise. The motivations for these charitable efforts included a desire for social stability, the wish to instil moral values in the population, the need to educate a future workforce.
